unit: Week 1 — Studio 1: Begin with your curiosity
title: From curiosity to a research problem: the four stops, and the tool that quietly changes your question
driving_question: How does a curiosity you actually care about become a research problem you could work on, without letting a tool choose it for you?
secondary_questions: What separates an experience, a curiosity, a topic, and a research problem? What do importance, feasibility, and possible contribution each ask? How do you catch a silent scope change or a confident fabrication inside a reply that sounds perfect?
claim_permitted: "This is the research problem I chose, these are the candidates I rejected, and here is the reason for each" — a problem you would still chase if every AI tool disappeared tomorrow.
claim_not_permitted: "This problem is new" — possible contribution stays provisional until Studio 3's evidence map; and any wording a tool introduced that you cannot account for.
rdss_reading: Required EDR|AI: the lesson 'From Curiosity to a Research Problem' (read before today) plus Studio 1's opening move, written by hand. Recommended RDSS: ch. 4 'Getting started' (book.declaredesign.org).
other_material: nb01 §Lecture 2 (Colab); the EDR|AI Studio 1 page; your four hand-written opening-move lines; notebooks/data/README.md
provenance: EDR|AI lesson 'From Curiosity to a Research Problem' + course dataset lapop_brazil | curiosity to a research problem | the four-stop funnel, a curiosity meeting real columns, and a structured divergence brainstorm with NEW marking | extended
concepts: experience → curiosity → topic → research problem; abduction (proposing what might explain a pattern); importance, feasibility, and possible contribution; the expected answer; silent scope change; confident fabrication; sycophantic agreement; the ownership test
python_r_dependency: pandas (load one course dataset, print one drawn respondent and three column means); no modeling
dataset_simulation: lapop_brazil (10,000 rows × 10 columns, a teaching resample with replacement — trust_military 5.16, trust_police 4.43, trust_supreme_court 4.05)
minute_dynamic: 0–7 SRL retrieval & challenge, still modeled from the instructor's chair: 0–3 a spoken 📝 drill on Monday's never-delegate list and the category that 'choose my semester question' belongs in, then one sentence each on line 1 of your opening move, 3–7 the challenge committed on paper — a tool turned a curiosity about sleep and health into a confident question about blue light and REM sleep, so name two distinct things wrong with it as YOUR question; 7–30 intensive applied AI laboratory: 7–12 🔮 predict first and then 🛠️ a curiosity meets real columns (load lapop_brazil, print one drawn respondent so you see what one row is, print the three trust averages sorted) with the bounded sentence read aloud before anyone moves on, 12–14 the four-stop funnel in one figure cell, stopping at the problem, 14–19 your own funnel in four lines with no tool, worked from the opening move you wrote by hand, 19–26 the lecture's ONE live AI prompt, the structured brainstorm run as a divergence partner, verified inside the same block by answering the five questions in your own words and circling every element marked NEW, 26–30 🔁 add your own constraint and rerun to see whether the NEW marks drop, then 🔬 interrogate the reply on claims, assumptions, missing information, and overstatements; 30–38 peer defense & adversarial questioning: 30–33 🧑‍⚖️ Human-Only Checkpoint with the tool closed, the ownership test in two lines, 33–35 ⚖️ commit to one of your two candidate problems and say in the same line why the other lost, 35–38 the stranger test, where you read only your problem sentence to a partner who knows nothing about it and write their stall down verbatim; 38–42 synthesis + instructor accuracy lock, modeled so the leads can replicate it: the funnel stops at the problem, the three tests in their exact wording, the two failures from the challenge named at last as silent scope change and confident fabrication, and one sentence on abduction as an argued position rather than a settled boundary; 42–50 project transfer: 🎯 your chosen research problem dated as version zero, the 🛡️ four-line close with contribution still provisional, the 📒 ledger row for the brainstorm exchange, and the spoken Claim Ticket.
hands_on_activity: Walk your own curiosity down the four-stop funnel by hand, then run the structured brainstorm as a divergence partner and keep or reject each direction with a written reason, circling every element the reply introduced.
practice: 📝 nb01 practice: sort six statements into experience / curiosity / topic / research problem, then say what the research problem names that the topic does not.
discussion_prompt: A reply hands you a sharper question than the one you wrote. How do you tell a real improvement from a silent scope change?
project_connection: The chosen research problem, dated as version zero, is the spine of Milestone 1, worked and submitted at this Friday's studio.
milestone_developed: M0 — Curiosity committed and the research problem, Book Milestone 1 v1 (dev)

student_prep: Your four opening-move lines, written BY HAND with no tool; the curiosity-to-problem lesson read through its worked example; laptop ready.
student_artifact: Own four-stop funnel + the chosen research-problem sentence + the brainstorm exchange with every NEW element marked and each direction kept or rejected with its reason
exit_ticket: Claim Ticket #2: my research problem in one breath — the specific unknown, and who would use the answer.
homework_next_milestone: Bring everything Milestone 1 needs to Friday's studio: the four hand-written lines, the brainstorm log with its NEW marks, the problem you chose, and your readiness evidence. Nothing new to draft tonight.

unit: Week 2 — Studio 2: Set your rules, shape your question
title: The question you declare: kind, reach, and the words your name signs
driving_question: What kind of answer does your question ask for, how far does it reach, and which word in your sentence fixes each?
secondary_questions: Why is prediction descriptive about unseen cases rather than a third kind? Why does a question's kind come from its own words and never from the data you happen to hold? What must a field card fix, and what must a claim boundary state?
inquiry: all four compass positions (description, generalization, prediction, causal reasoning)
srl_slot: SRL slot 02 (randomly assigned at semester start)
srl_focus: Challenge: a colleague is proud of one question — how common is burnout among nurses, and does working night shifts cause it — so find the seam and label each half by kind.
claim_permitted: "My question is a ___ inquiry reaching ___, because of these exact words" — and, when no design can isolate it, "causal, currently unidentified."
claim_not_permitted: "Descriptive, because I only have survey data" — the kind is fixed by the question's words, never by the data you happen to hold.

unit: Week 3 — Studio 3: Ground it in verified evidence
title: A lead is not a source: retrieve it, read it, and find out what it actually supports
driving_question: How do you tell a source that exists from a source that says what you claim, and when have you actually earned the word gap?
secondary_questions: What promotes a lead to a source? What do backward and forward citation searches each find? What may you honestly write when a search comes up empty?
srl_slot: SRL slot 03 (randomly assigned at semester start)
srl_focus: Puzzle: two sentences rest on the same real number from the same real file, and the source can carry only one of them — vote in writing before the data README is opened.
claim_permitted: "Source S exists, I retrieved and opened it, and it supports exactly this sentence" — and "across the sources I retrieved and verified, none addresses my question."
claim_not_permitted: "Nothing is known about my topic" from a search that stopped early, and any source cited for a claim you have not read inside the source itself.
rdss_reading: Required EDR|AI: 'Research Builds on Research' and 'Finding and Verifying Prior Evidence' (read before today, with the first lesson's candidate list already built, every row marked lead). Recommended RDSS: ch. 4 'Getting started', on situating a design in a literature (book.declaredesign.org).
other_material: nb03 (Colab); your colleague's evidence registry + search log (simulated-case banner, handed out in class); project/colleague/audit_protocol.md + audit_rubric.md; Purdue Libraries database portal; Google Scholar; notebooks/data/README.md
provenance: EDR|AI Studio 3 lessons (research-builds, verifying-prior-evidence) + Synthetic Colleague scored audit 2 of 10 + notebooks/data/README.md | grounding the question in verified evidence | the two-check retrieval discipline, a seeded mischaracterized source, and the evidence-map builder | extended
concepts: lead versus source; the two separate checks (does it exist, does it say this); citation hallucination; mischaracterized source; claim-evidence-source alignment; backward and forward citation searches; snowballing; the four evidence types (descriptive, generalization, predictive, causal); the bounded gap sentence and its honesty test; contradiction as data, not a verdict
python_r_dependency: pandas (fill a claims table and a relations table), networkx (the evidence map draws itself), numpy (the seeded two-engine retrieval run)
dataset_simulation: lapop_brazil read alongside notebooks/data/README.md for the opening vote (trust_police mean 4.43 in a teaching resample), plus a seeded two-engine simulation (SEED 464: 15 candidates → 9 retrievable → 6 verified, snowball 6, 9, 13, 22) and the student's own retrieved sources
minute_dynamic: 0–7 SRL retrieval & challenge: 0–3 🧩 the two-sentence vote on one real number from a file that ships with this course, committed in writing before the README is opened, closing on the line the room will hear four more times today, that a source can pass 'does it exist' and fail 'does it say this', 3–5 📝 a spoken drill labeling three source-claims aligned, mischaracterized, or unverifiable, 5–7 audit move 1 Commit, marking every row of your colleague's evidence registry before anything is checked; 7–30 intensive applied AI laboratory carrying the SCORED colleague audit (audit 2 of 10): 7–8 🔮 predict first on how many of 15 AI-suggested candidates survive both checks, 8–11 move 2 Locate, where a row number and a quoted sentence count and a feeling does not, 11–18 move 3 Verify by hand, searching the exact title in quotation marks in the library database and in Google Scholar, then reading the abstract, the design section, and the results against the sentence the registry attributes to the source, 18–24 the lecture's ONE live AI exchange, run only after you have retrieved the source yourself, with 🔬 every quoted line checked against the paper open on your screen and a 🔁 flip of the framing named aloud with its drift predicted, 24–27 move 4 Diagnose, naming the flaw as a mischaracterized source and saying which of the two checks it failed, 27–30 🛠️ the two-engine reveal read against your prediction, 15 candidates to 9 retrievable to 6 verified with the snowball growing 6, 9, 13, 22; 30–38 peer defense & adversarial questioning: 30–33 move 5 Repair, the smallest defensible correction with its new claim boundary, 33–36 swap repairs and put two questions to your partner, show me where you opened it and read me the sentence in the paper that carries your repair, 36–38 move 6 Calibrate, defending one element that looked suspicious and is sound; 38–42 SRL synthesis + instructor accuracy lock (audit move 7): the room's finding stated in one sentence, the seeded flaw confirmed, the corrected claim stated aloud, and the likely false positives named so nothing wrong enters a ledger; 42–50 project transfer: ⚖️ choose the one defensible gap of three and say why the other two are unfinished searches wearing a gap's clothes, 🧑‍⚖️ a Human-Only Checkpoint with the tool closed on which of your own rows is verified and which is still a lead, 🎯 your bounded contribution line into the dossier, the 🛡️ four-line close, the 📒 ledger row, and the spoken Claim Ticket.
hands_on_activity: Run both checks by hand on the located registry rows — search the exact title in quotation marks, open what resolves, and read the abstract, design, and results against the sentence attributed to the source — then write the smallest defensible repair and its new boundary.
practice: 📝 nb03 practice: label three source-claims aligned, mischaracterized, or unverifiable, and name the step that decided each.
discussion_prompt: Two of your verified sources flatly contradict each other. What do you record, and what could make both of them right?
project_connection: The bounded contribution line you write today is what Friday's evidence base has to earn: the registry, the search log, and the map exist to support that one sentence.

unit: Week 4 — Studio 4: Declare and diagnose provisionally
title: The four parts of a design, and the pile of answers behind every number
driving_question: What are the four parts every research design must have, and why does the same recipe, run twice, return two different numbers?
secondary_questions: What is an estimand, what is an estimator, and what is an estimate? What does a 95% interval actually promise? What changes when the same 60 interviews are collected in six clusters instead of at random?
srl_slot: SRL slot 04 (randomly assigned at semester start)
srl_focus: Puzzle: the same 60-person survey, run twice in the same month on the same declared population, returns 4.58 and 4.23, and the supervisor asks which run is the mistake — then the team proposes 10 people in each of 6 municipalities instead.
claim_permitted: "My estimand is this quantity in the world, over this population, setting, and time, and my estimator is a recipe a stranger could run without asking me a question."
claim_not_permitted: "There is a 95% chance the true average lies between 3.90 and 4.93" — the recipe holds the 95% property, and only while its assumptions hold.
rdss_reading: Required EDR|AI: 'Model, Inquiry, Data Strategy, and Answer Strategy' and 'Uncertainty Before You Need It' (read before today). Recommended RDSS: ch. 2 'What is a research design?' and ch. 5 'Declaring designs' (book.declaredesign.org).
other_material: nb04 §Lecture 1 (Colab); your declared question and evidence base; the MIDA four-box schematic cell; notebooks/data/README.md
provenance: EDR|AI Studio 4 lessons (mida, uncertainty-foundations) + course dataset lapop_brazil declared as a teaching population | the anatomy of a design and the shape of chance | MIDA run against one declared world, a seeded sampling distribution, and a clustered-collection contrast | extended
concepts: Model, Inquiry, Data strategy, Answer strategy, and the alignment rule; a causal question a design cannot reach stays causal and currently unidentified; estimand, estimator, estimate; the sampling distribution as a pile of answers; standard error; what a confidence interval promises and what it does not; the independent unit and the assumption that licenses it
python_r_dependency: numpy + pandas (declare a population and run one estimator 2,000 times), matplotlib (the pile of estimates with the estimand marked)
dataset_simulation: lapop_brazil (10,000 rows × 10 columns) declared as the teaching population — the estimand is the mean trust_police of 4.427 over the rows in this file and never a fact about a country — with a seeded run (SEED 464: run 1 = 4.583, run 2 = 4.233, spread 0.263, coverage 93.6%) and a clustered second run over its 107 municipalities (81.0% versus 90.2%)
minute_dynamic: 0–9 SRL research puzzle with no AI: the same survey run twice returning 4.58 and 4.23, both answers written before anyone speaks, then the cluster variant that keeps the same 60 interviews and the same arithmetic, with the one thing the room agrees on and the one thing it splits on put on the board at minute 7 and left unresolved; 9–31 guided AI research-partner investigation: 9–13 MIDA named against the puzzle's own declaration using the four-box schematic, closing on the alignment sentence you reuse all week, that because my data strategy samples X, my answer strategy's number speaks to Y, 13–16 estimand, estimator, and estimate defined against the declared file, where 4.427 does not move and 4.583 does, 16–18 🔮 predict first on how far a typical 60-person run lands from the estimand and why, 18–24 🛠️ run the study, 2,000 seeded runs printing the estimand, the first two single runs, the centre and spread of the pile, and the share of intervals that caught the estimand, 24–31 the lecture's ONE live AI prompt on your OWN question after a hand-written commitment, asking for your estimand as a quantity in the world and your estimator as a recipe, with no numbers and no advice; 31–43 human verification + instructor formalization: 31–34 🔍 read the evidence in two lines, what the pile establishes about this recipe under these assumptions and what it never establishes about the world, 34–37 standard error and the interval's real promise, with the sentence to refuse written on the board beside the true one, 37–41 🛠️ the puzzle's resolution, where the same 60 interviews collected as 6 municipalities of 10 leave the naive interval catching the estimand 81.0% of the time instead of the promised 95% while the municipality-level interval catches it 90.2%, and where the direction of the correction is not automatic, 41–43 📝 spoken practice on which reading of a 95% interval is warranted; 43–50 decision & defense: ⚖️ one written line naming the unit your uncertainty will treat as independent and the single assumption that licenses it, 🎯 your estimand as a quantity in the world with a population, a setting, and a time, the 🛡️ four-line close, the 📒 ledger row written in the room, and the spoken Claim Ticket.
hands_on_activity: Declare the file as a population, run its estimator 2,000 times, and read the pile — where it sits, how wide it is, and how often the interval recipe actually caught the estimand — then write your own estimand and estimator and rewrite both in your own words.
practice: 📝 nb04 practice, spoken: an approximate 95% interval runs 3.90 to 4.93, so which reading is warranted, and why is the probability-about-the-truth reading the trap this lecture exists to prevent?
discussion_prompt: Your supervisor asks which of the two runs was the mistake. What do you say, and what number should have been reported next to the first one?
project_connection: Your estimand and your independent unit are Contract v0 fields, and both are written before any tool touches them.

unit: Week 4 — Studio 4: Declare and diagnose provisionally
title: Diagnose it before it costs you anything, then find out whether you are allowed to run it
driving_question: How will your design actually behave before you spend a semester running it, and who decides whether you may run it at all?
secondary_questions: What does a power number mean without its test and its threshold? Which of bias, wobble, and power can more units buy, and which can they never touch? What makes 'the data are public and we removed the names' not a permission determination?
inquiry: causal + generalization (diagnosis, permission, and the claim boundary)
srl_slot: SRL slot 05 (randomly assigned at semester start)
srl_focus: Challenge: the colleague's Research Contract v0 claims 80% power with 10 units per arm, names no test and no threshold anywhere, records that no redesign was needed, and calls its permission cleared because the data are public.
claim_permitted: "My diagnosed design has these properties under this named test and threshold, so it can support this claim and not that one, and my permission status is declared with its authority."
claim_not_permitted: "Our design has 80% power" with no test and no threshold stated, and "cleared: the data are public and we removed the names" asserted rather than determined.
rdss_reading: Required EDR|AI: 'Declaring and Diagnosing a Research Design' and 'Research Ethics and Data Governance' (read before today). Recommended RDSS: ch. 10 'Diagnosing designs' and ch. 11 'Redesigning' (book.declaredesign.org).
cb_reading: optional: callingbullshit.org case on an underpowered or invalid design
other_material: nb04 §Lecture 2 (Colab); your colleague's Research Contract v0 (simulated-case banner, handed out in class); project/colleague/audit_protocol.md + audit_rubric.md; the columns you plan to collect for your own project
provenance: EDR|AI Studio 4 lessons (declare-diagnose, ethics-data-governance) + Synthetic Colleague scored audit 3 of 10 + course dataset la_voter_file | diagnosis and permission | a rerun diagnosis with its decision rule printed beside the power number, and a uniqueness check on a public record about identifiable people | extended
concepts: declare, diagnose, redesign; bias, wobble, and power, and what more units can and cannot buy; the decision rule and threshold a power number needs; quasi-identifiers and re-identification; data minimisation and coarsening; the four permission statuses and the competent authority; the four governance decisions and the stop plan; identify versus associate
python_r_dependency: numpy (rerun the seeded diagnosis over three declared designs), pandas (the uniqueness table over quasi-identifiers)
dataset_simulation: an inline seeded mentoring world (SEED 464 — 10 per arm: bias −0.053, power 9.3%; 600 per arm randomized: bias −0.006, power 93.5%; 600 per arm confounded: bias +6.366, power 100.0%) plus la_voter_file (1,000 rows × 4 columns — party alone 0.4% unique, party + age + census_tract 99.6%, coarsened to 19.9%)
minute_dynamic: 0–7 SRL retrieval & challenge: 0–3 📝 a spoken drill from memory with no notes on estimand versus estimate, what the 95% in an interval actually describes, and the one thing the clustered run changed and the one it did not, 3–7 the colleague's Research Contract v0 handed out and audit move 1 Commit, a written verdict on each of its five headline claims before anything is checked; 7–30 intensive applied AI laboratory carrying the SCORED colleague audit (audit 3 of 10): 7–9 move 2 Locate, an exact line, cell, or table row behind every unsupported or uncertain mark, 9–11 the lecture's ONE live AI prompt fired now so it works while the room moves on, asking for the questions a research ethics committee would ask about your own plan with no conclusions and no reassurance, 11–19 move 3 station A, rerunning the diagnosis with its decision rule and threshold printed in the same cell as the power number, where the contract's 80% claim meets a declared design that detects the effect 9 times in 100, 19–25 station B, running the uniqueness check on a public voter file until 99.6% of rows are unique on three ordinary columns and coarsening brings that to 19.9%, with 🔍 two lines on what public availability does and does not establish, 25–28 🔁 rewriting the committee prompt to name your own units and your actual route to the data, then 🔬 interrogating whether it stated a conclusion anywhere and quoting the exact words if it did, 28–30 moves 4 and 5, Diagnose the flaw by its rule and Repair it with the smallest defensible correction and its new claim boundary; 30–38 peer defense & adversarial questioning: each person states their verdict, their exact locator, and the check they actually ran while the room attacks, and audit move 6 Calibrate is scored here, defending one element that looked suspicious and is sound against three planted traps, including a provisional operationalization, which is correct at this studio; 38–42 SRL synthesis + instructor accuracy lock: the room's findings in three lines, the seeded flaw confirmed, the corrected version stated aloud, and every record corrected now, because the audit ends when the record is corrected and not when the flaw is found; 42–50 project transfer: ⚖️ which of bias, wobble, or power is your design's biggest threat and the single redesign it demands, 🧑‍⚖️ a Human-Only Checkpoint with the tool closed declaring one permission status, the competent authority who covers student projects, and the date you will contact them, 🎯 the one Contract v0 line that changes because of today, the 🛡️ four-line close, the 📒 ledger row carrying your AI boundary, and the spoken Claim Ticket.
hands_on_activity: Rerun the colleague's diagnosis with the decision rule printed beside the power number, run the uniqueness check on a public voter file and then coarsen it, and write the smallest defensible repair for the flaw you located.
practice: 📝 nb04 practice: for three designs, label the biggest threat bias, wobble, or power, and name the one redesign that most reduces it.
discussion_prompt: A dataset is public and the names are gone. What has that established about your project, and what has it not?
project_connection: Three Contract v0 lines leave with you today: your diagnosed threat with its redesign, your declared permission status with its authority, and your AI boundary.

claim_permitted: "My data reached me by [route], were produced by [source] using [method] on [date] under [terms], and here is the record that shows it" — a provenance-backed acquisition claim.
claim_not_permitted: "It was public on the internet, so it is fine to use" — availability is not permission, a dataset is governed by its licence or terms, and a file with no provenance record cannot underwrite any claim.

unit: Week 11 — Studio 11: Reproduce and package
title: The cold run: does your number come back without you in the room?
driving_question: A package's write-up says 4 points. You clear the runtime, press Restart and Run All, and 3.41 prints. Is that a rounding quibble or a finding?

claim_not_permitted: "It ran clean, so the claim is sound" — a package can reproduce perfectly and still be wrong; and a headline quoted from the friendlier end of an undisclosed choice instead of reported as a spread.

claim_not_permitted: "Independent reproduction confirmed" over the author's own rerun on the author's own machine — and any package whose load cell names a path only its author has.
